title: Toxic Alcohols and Salicylate: Reading the Osmolal and Anion Gaps
summary: Calculate the osmolal gap and know its limits, link methanol, ethylene glycol and isopropanol to their metabolites and acid-base pictures, and read salicylate poisoning as respiratory alkalosis followed by anion gap metabolic acidosis that needs serial levels.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 24 Hits 4 (osmolal gap formula and toxic alcohols), 5 (methanol, ethylene glycol and isopropanol patterns and fomepizole) and 15 (salicylate acid-base sequence), checked against Gallagher 2019, Lynd 2008, Greene 2020, Ghannoum 2023 (EXTRIP ethylene glycol), Sidlak 2025 and Samlan 2008 (all read as Europe PMC full text). Qualified against sources: an osmolal gap is insensitive and a normal gap does not exclude a toxic alcohol (register flag rv-osmolal-gap-normal-not-exclude); tinnitus occurs in acute overdoses, not only chronic toxicity (rv-salicylate-tinnitus-acute); no reliable salicylate nomogram exists, so the Done nomogram is not taught (rv-salicylate-done-nomogram). The EXTRIP salicylate and methanol papers themselves were not open access and were not read; their criteria are cited only as reported by the reviews. Not taught: Number Vault lethal doses, ethanol legal limit, treatment dosing.

objectives: Calculate the osmolal gap and state why a normal gap does not exclude a toxic alcohol.
Match methanol, ethylene glycol and isopropanol to their metabolites, acid-base pattern and laboratory clues.
Describe the salicylate acid-base sequence and the laboratory pitfalls in measuring salicylate.

scenes.title: Three overdoses, three gaps
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three emergency patients after unknown ingestions. (1) Blurred vision, pH 7.08, anion gap 30, osmolal gap 34. (2) Deeply drowsy, pH 7.40, normal anion gap, osmolal gap 30, acetone in serum and urine. (3) Breathing fast, pH 7.49, PCO2 low, says sounds are muffled. Question token: “Which poison, and what does each gap say?”

cues.text: Three patients arrive after unknown ingestions. The first has blurred vision, a pH of seven point zero eight, and both an anion gap and an osmolal gap.
The second is deeply drowsy with a normal pH, a normal anion gap, a big osmolal gap, and acetone in blood and urine. The third is breathing fast, alkalemic, and says sounds are muffled.
Which poison is each one, and what is each gap telling you?

props.label: Which poison? What does each gap say?

scenes.title: Measured minus calculated
scenes.altText: Formula card: osmolal gap = measured osmolality (osmometer, ideally freezing point depression) minus calculated osmolality, where calculated = 2 × Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (mg/dL units). Ethanol card: ethanol also raises measured osmolality; one review adds ethanol (mg/dL)/4.25 to the calculation, and an ethanol level must be checked. Range card: “normal” gap is quoted as under 10 to under 20 depending on source; a gap above 20 without another explanation is suspicious for a toxic alcohol. Other-causes card: ketoacidosis, kidney failure, lactic acidosis, mannitol, shock, and propylene glycol (from intravenous lorazepam or activated charcoal); and a normal gap does not exclude a toxic alcohol.

cues.text: The osmolal gap is measured osmolality, from an osmometer, ideally by freezing point depression, minus calculated osmolality: two times sodium, plus glucose over eighteen, plus BUN over two point eight.

Small molecules that the formula does not count raise the measured value. Ethanol is one of them, so always check an ethanol level; one review adds ethanol divided by four point two five to the calculation.
Quoted normal limits vary, from under ten to under twenty. A gap above twenty with no other explanation is suspicious for a toxic alcohol.
But ketoacidosis, kidney failure, lactic acidosis, mannitol, shock and propylene glycol from intravenous lorazepam or charcoal also raise it. And a normal gap does not rule a toxic alcohol out.

scenes.title: The liver turns alcohol into acid
scenes.altText: Metabolism cards. Methanol → (alcohol dehydrogenase) formaldehyde → (aldehyde dehydrogenase) formic acid: high anion gap metabolic acidosis and optic nerve injury, with visual disturbances in 29–72% of cases. Ethylene glycol → glycolaldehyde → glycolic acid (main cause of the acidosis) → oxalic acid → calcium oxalate crystals in kidney and urine (kidney injury); crystals are neither sensitive nor specific. Isopropanol → acetone only: osmolal gap with acetone in blood and urine but usually no acidosis (hypotension can add lactic acidosis). Treatment token: fomepizole, a competitive alcohol dehydrogenase blocker, is the treatment of choice; ethanol is the alternative; hemodialysis by EXTRIP criteria. Time arrow: early the osmolal gap is high and the anion gap normal; as the alcohol is metabolised the osmolal gap falls and the anion gap rises.

cues.text: The parent alcohols are not the main danger. Alcohol dehydrogenase turns methanol into formaldehyde, then formic acid. Formic acid causes a severe anion gap acidosis and injures the optic nerve, which is why vision blurs.

Ethylene glycol becomes glycolic acid, the main driver of its acidosis, then oxalic acid, which deposits calcium oxalate crystals in the kidney and urine. Crystals help, but their absence does not rule it out.
Isopropanol is turned into acetone and stops there. Acetone is not an acid, so you see an osmolal gap and acetone, usually without acidosis.

Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and is the treatment of choice; ethanol is the alternative, and dialysis follows set criteria. And timing matters: as the alcohol is metabolised, the osmolal gap falls while the anion gap rises.

props.label: Fomepizole blocks ADH (choice) · ethanol alternative · dialysis by criteria
Over time: osmolal gap ↓ · anion gap ↑

scenes.title: Salicylate: two disorders at once
scenes.altText: Salicylate cards (Sidlak 2025). Early: salicylate stimulates the brainstem and arterial chemoreceptors → fast, deep breathing → respiratory alkalosis. Later: uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation → anion gap metabolic acidosis; classic picture is a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus anion gap metabolic acidosis, which co-ingested sedatives can blunt. Tinnitus or reduced hearing also occurs after acute single overdoses (Samlan 2008: documented in 99 of 213 cases with a record, with higher initial and peak levels), but not in every patient. Lab card: one early level can be undetectable and peaks can be delayed, so measure serial levels about every 2 hours; no reliable nomogram exists, the Done nomogram included; some chloride methods read falsely high, giving a falsely normal anion gap. Hook answers: (1) methanol; (2) isopropanol; (3) salicylate.

cues.text: Salicylate does two things. First it stimulates the brainstem breathing centre and chemoreceptors, so the patient breathes fast and deep: respiratory alkalosis.

Then it uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis builds. The classic gas is a mixed disorder, though sedatives taken with it can blunt the fast breathing. Tinnitus or muffled hearing occurs in acute overdoses too.

In the lab, one early level can be undetectable and peaks can come late, so repeat levels about every two hours. No reliable nomogram exists, and that includes the old Done nomogram. And some chloride methods read falsely high, hiding the anion gap.
Back to the hook: patient one is methanol, patient two is isopropanol, and patient three is salicylate.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal osmolal gap rules out a toxic alcohol” (✓ the gap is insensitive, has a wide normal range, and falls as the alcohol is metabolised); “Isopropanol causes the same severe acidosis as methanol” (✓ it stops at acetone, giving an osmolal gap and ketosis with usually no acidosis); “One salicylate level plotted on the Done nomogram settles it” (✓ no reliable nomogram exists; repeat levels and follow the acid-base status).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal osmolal gap rules out a toxic alcohol. No: the gap is insensitive, its normal range is wide, and it shrinks as the alcohol is metabolised.
Trap two: isopropanol causes the same severe acidosis as methanol. No: it stops at acetone, so expect an osmolal gap and acetone, usually without acidosis.
Trap three: one salicylate level on the Done nomogram settles it. No: no reliable nomogram exists. Repeat levels and follow the blood gas.

scenes.title: Parents make osmoles, children make acid
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “PARENTS make osmoles, CHILDREN make acid.” The parent alcohol (methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropanol) is a small molecule that raises the osmolal gap; its metabolic children (formic acid, glycolic acid) raise the anion gap, except isopropanol’s child acetone, which is not an acid. Salicylate: “breathe first, acid later.” Tokens: parent = osmolal gap · child = anion gap · acetone = no acid. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: parents make osmoles, children make acid. The parent alcohol raises the osmolal gap; its metabolites, formic and glycolic acid, raise the anion gap. Isopropanol’s child, acetone, is not an acid. For salicylate: breathe first, acid later.

Where it breaks: acetone still adds osmoles; ethylene glycol also harms through oxalate crystals, not just acid; with isopropanol, low blood pressure can add a lactic acidosis; and salicylate’s acidosis comes from uncoupled metabolism, not from an acid child.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Osmolal gap = measured − (2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8) · parent alcohol early, acids later · normal gap does not exclude”, “Salicylate = respiratory alkalosis then anion gap acidosis · serial levels, no reliable nomogram”.

cues.text: An osmolal gap flags the parent alcohol early while the anion gap rises as methanol and ethylene glycol become acids, isopropanol makes acetone usually without acidosis, and salicylate gives respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis that needs serial levels rather than a nomogram.

props.label: Osm gap = parent alcohol early · anion gap = acids later
Salicylate: alkalosis → acidosis · serial levels, no nomogram

explanation.what: Plain language: some poisons are small molecules that crowd the blood with extra particles, which the osmometer counts but the formula does not; the liver then turns some of them into acids. Salicylate first makes people breathe hard, then poisons cell energy production and acid builds up. Scientific terms: measured osmolality (freezing point depression), calculated osmolality, osmolal gap, anion gap, alcohol dehydrogenase, formic acid, glycolic acid, calcium oxalate, acetone, fomepizole, respiratory alkalosis, uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, pseudohyperchloremia.
explanation.why: Direct toxic alcohol measurement by gas chromatography is often a send-out test, so the osmolal gap, anion gap and acid-base status guide early treatment. Salicylate levels can be undetectable early and peak late, so a single level can mislead.
explanation.measure: Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (mg/dL); osmolal gap = measured − calculated; check ethanol (one review adds ethanol/4.25). Quoted normal gap under 10 to under 20; over 20 unexplained is suspicious. Salicylate: serial levels about every 2 hours with blood gases; some chloride methods read falsely high with salicylate, hiding the anion gap.
explanation.differs: Methanol (formic acid, visual injury) vs ethylene glycol (glycolic acid, calcium oxalate crystals, kidney injury) vs isopropanol (acetone, osmolal gap usually without acidosis); early (high osmolal gap, normal anion gap) vs late (lower osmolal gap, high anion gap); salicylate early respiratory alkalosis vs later mixed anion gap metabolic acidosis.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate an osmolal gap; identify the alcohol from crystals, vision changes or acetone without acidosis; recognise the mixed acid-base disorder of salicylate; reject “normal gap excludes toxic alcohol” and single-level nomogram reasoning.

comparisons.title: Methanol vs ethylene glycol
comparisons.distinguisher: Eyes vs kidneys and crystals; both give osmolal and anion gaps.

comparisons.title: Isopropanol vs methanol and ethylene glycol
comparisons.distinguisher: Acetone without acidosis vs acid metabolites.

comparisons.title: Salicylate early vs later
comparisons.distinguisher: Breathing drive first, metabolic failure later; often both together.

mnemonic.text: PARENTS make osmoles, CHILDREN make acid: the parent alcohol raises the osmolal gap, its metabolites raise the anion gap, and isopropanol’s child acetone is not an acid. Salicylate: breathe first, acid later.
mnemonic.explanation: Links the time course of the two gaps to metabolism, and the salicylate sequence to breathing then acid.
mnemonic.limitation: Acetone still adds osmoles; ethylene glycol also injures through oxalate crystals; with isopropanol, hypotension can add lactic acidosis; salicylate acidosis comes from uncoupled metabolism rather than an acid metabolite.

questions.stem: A patient has Na 140 mEq/L, glucose 90 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, ethanol undetectable, and a measured serum osmolality of 320 mOsm/kg by freezing point depression. What is the osmolal gap?

options.rationale: Correct. Calculated = 2 × 140 + 90/18 + 14/2.8 = 280 + 5 + 5 = 290; 320 − 290 = 30, a gap suspicious for a toxic alcohol if unexplained.
Incorrect. A gap of 10 would need a calculated osmolality near 310, but the correct calculation gives 280 + 5 + 5 = 290.
Incorrect. This omits the glucose term (5); both glucose/18 and BUN/2.8 must be added.
Incorrect. This forgets to double sodium; sodium is multiplied by 2 to account for its accompanying anions.

questions.stem: A drowsy patient has an elevated osmolal gap, normal arterial pH, a normal anion gap, and acetone in serum and urine. Which ingestion best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. Isopropanol is metabolised only to acetone, which is not an acid: osmolal gap and acetone, usually without acidosis.
Incorrect. Methanol forms formic acid and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Incorrect. Ethylene glycol forms glycolic and oxalic acids, giving an anion gap acidosis and calcium oxalate crystals.
Incorrect. Salicylate classically gives respiratory alkalosis and then an anion gap metabolic acidosis; an osmolal gap with acetone and a normal pH fits isopropanol.

questions.stem: Two hours after a reported aspirin overdose, the first serum salicylate is low and the patient is well. What is the best laboratory approach?

options.text: Repeat salicylate levels about every 2 hours with blood gases
options.rationale: Correct. Early levels can be low or undetectable and peaks can be delayed, so serial levels with acid-base status are needed.

options.text: Plot the single level on the Done nomogram
options.rationale: Incorrect. No reliable salicylate nomogram exists, the Done nomogram included.

options.text: Rule out toxicity because there is no tinnitus
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tinnitus is not present in every patient, and its absence does not exclude toxicity.

options.text: Rule out toxicity because the anion gap is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. The acidosis can develop later, and some chloride methods read falsely high with salicylate, hiding the anion gap.

references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Gallagher N, Edwards FJ. The Diagnosis and Management of Toxic Alcohol Poisoning in the Emergency Department: A Review Article. Adv J Emerg Med. 2019;3(3):e28. doi:10.22114/ajem.v0i0.153
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Calculated osmolality formula and ethanol term (ethanol/4.25); osmol gap normal range varies (<10 to <20) and >20 suspicious; alternative causes (ketoacidosis, renal failure, lactic acidosis, mannitol, shock); normal gap does not exclude; inverse time course of osmol and anion gaps; methanol to formaldehyde and formic acid, optic nerve injury, visual disturbances in 29–72%; ethylene glycol to glycolic and oxalic acid, calcium oxalate crystals neither sensitive nor specific; isopropanol to acetone, osmol gap usually without acidosis, hypotension may add lactic acidosis; fomepizole as treatment of choice, ethanol alternative, EXTRIP dialysis criteria as reported; gas chromatography as gold standard, often send-out.

references.citation: Lynd LD, Richardson KJ, Purssell RA, Abu-Laban RB, Brubacher JR, Lepik KJ, Sivilotti ML. An evaluation of the osmole gap as a screening test for toxic alcohol poisoning. BMC Emerg Med. 2008;8:5. doi:10.1186/1471-227x-8-5
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Osmole gap as measured osmolality (freezing point depression) minus calculated value; wide normal range makes it insensitive to small but toxic concentrations; results do not support use of the osmole gap in isolation.

references.citation: Greene HR, Krasowski MD. Correlation of osmolal gap with measured concentrations of acetone, ethylene glycol, isopropanol, methanol, and propylene glycol in patients at an academic medical center. Toxicol Rep. 2020;7:81-88. doi:10.1016/j.toxrep.2019.12.005
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Measured osmolality ideally by freezing point depression; propylene glycol (intravenous lorazepam, activated charcoal) and acetone also raise the osmolal gap; isopropanol metabolised to acetone; gas chromatography as gold standard.

references.citation: Ghannoum M, Gosselin S, Hoffman RS, et al. Extracorporeal treatment for ethylene glycol poisoning: systematic review and recommendations from the EXTRIP workgroup. Crit Care. 2023;27(1):56. doi:10.1186/s13054-022-04227-2
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Ethylene glycol oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase to glycolaldehyde then glycolate; glycolate contributes to the acidemia; calcium oxalate deposition causes kidney injury.

references.citation: Sidlak AM, Spadaro A, Koyfman A, Long B. Acute Salicylate Toxicity: A Narrative Review for Emergency Clinicians. Cureus. 2025;17(9):e91505. doi:10.7759/cureus.91505
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Early respiratory alkalosis from brainstem and arterial chemoreceptor effects; metabolic acidosis from uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation; classic mixed disorder, blunted by sedative co-ingestion; tinnitus in acute salicylism largely presenting as diminished hearing, and not found in all patients (the review’s 78% and ~30 mg/dL figures come from a 1973 therapeutic-dosing study, Mongan 1973, so they are not taught as acute-overdose figures); early levels may be undetectable and peaks delayed, serial levels at two-hour intervals; no reliable salicylate nomogram (citing Dugandzic 1989 on the Done nomogram); falsely elevated chloride on some analyzers giving a falsely normal anion gap.

references.citation: Samlan SR, Jordan MT, Chan SB, Wahl MS, Rubin RL. Tinnitus as a measure of salicylate toxicity in the overdose setting. West J Emerg Med. 2008;9(3):146-149.
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Tinnitus and/or hearing loss documented in 99 of 213 single-overdose cases with a record; those patients had higher initial and peak salicylate levels (mean initial 48.3 vs 30.2 mg/dL); the paper notes earlier evidence came from chronic therapeutic dosing (acute, not only chronic, setting).

claims.text: Osmolal gap = measured (osmometer, ideally freezing point depression) − (2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8); ethanol must be checked and can be added (ethanol/4.25).

Normal gap quoted as <10 to <20; >20 unexplained suspicious; other causes include ketoacidosis, kidney failure, lactic acidosis, mannitol, shock, propylene glycol; a normal gap does not exclude a toxic alcohol; gaps change inversely over time.
Methanol to formaldehyde to formic acid; anion gap acidosis; optic nerve injury and visual disturbances; fomepizole preferred, ethanol alternative, dialysis by criteria.
Ethylene glycol to glycolic acid (acidosis) and oxalate; calcium oxalate crystals and kidney injury; crystals neither sensitive nor specific.
Isopropanol metabolised to acetone only; osmolal gap with acetone, usually no acidosis; hypotension can add lactic acidosis.
Salicylate: early respiratory alkalosis (brainstem, chemoreceptors), then anion gap metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation; sedatives can blunt the alkalosis.
Tinnitus occurs in acute overdose; serial levels about every 2 hours; no reliable nomogram; falsely high chloride can hide the anion gap.
Reviewer: tinnitus/hearing loss flags chronic salicylate toxicity; use the Done nomogram.
claims.note: Not taught as stated. Sidlak 2025 and Samlan 2008 describe tinnitus after acute single overdoses; Sidlak 2025 states no reliable salicylate nomogram exists, citing a 1989 evaluation of the Done nomogram (Dugandzic 1989, not itself read). The lesson teaches serial levels instead.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 24 Hit 4 says an unexplained osmolal gap means a toxic alcohol until proven otherwise, but gives no limit on the negative side. Gallagher 2019 and Lynd 2008 describe the gap as insensitive with a wide normal range, falling as the alcohol is metabolised, so a normal gap does not exclude a toxic alcohol; the lesson teaches this (register flag rv-osmolal-gap-normal-not-exclude).

Ch. 24 Hit 15 says tinnitus/hearing loss flags chronic salicylate toxicity. Sidlak 2025 and Samlan 2008 describe tinnitus or hearing loss after acute single overdoses as well; the lesson teaches that it occurs in acute overdose too (register flag rv-salicylate-tinnitus-acute).

Ch. 24 Hit 15 says to use the Done nomogram. Sidlak 2025 states no reliable salicylate nomogram exists and recommends serial levels; the lesson does not teach the Done nomogram (register flag rv-salicylate-done-nomogram).
